title: 26 U.S. Code Section 41(d)(2) Business Component Test
description: 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2), the business component test, applies the Four-Part Test separately to each product, process, software or invention.
summary: 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2), the business component test, requires U.S. taxpayers claiming the federal R&D tax credit to apply the Four-Part Test separately to each product, process, software, technique, formula, or invention. When a project fails, the shrinking-back rule isolates qualifying sub-components, but only if contemporaneous, component-level time-tracking records exist.

body.text: 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2), the business component test, requires U.S. taxpayers claiming the federal R&D tax credit to apply the Four-Part Test separately to each product, process, software, technique, formula, or invention. When a project fails, the shrinking-back rule isolates qualifying sub-components, but only if contemporaneous, component-level time-tracking records exist.
Executive Summary and Statutory Architecture

Under the United States Internal Revenue Code, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2) establishes the foundational structural unit of analysis for claiming the federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit by mandating that statutory qualification criteria be applied separately to each discrete "business component" developed or improved by a taxpayer. The statute defines a business component under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention that is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. When a macro-level project fails to satisfy the statutory qualification requirements of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2) mandates that the technical evaluation "shrink back" iteratively to the next most significant subset of elements until a qualifying sub-component is isolated or the most basic element of the product is reached and fails to qualify.

The legislative policy governing 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2) prevents taxpayers from bundling non-qualifying commercial production, routine engineering, or cosmetic modifications with genuine experimental research in an effort to subsidize standard operational expenditures. Both federal jurisprudence and state revenue conformity frameworks—most notably in Indiana, California, and Idaho—demonstrate that the Business Component Test functions as a strict evidentiary gatekeeper. The structural interaction between component identification and substantiation creates an asymmetric audit risk profile in which taxpayers relying on macro-level project accounting, retrospective percentage estimations, or an "all or nothing" litigation posture without sub-component time-tracking records forfeit their ability to invoke the shrinking-back rule, resulting in the complete disallowance of claimed qualified research expenses (QREs).
Federal Legislative Genesis and Regulatory Evolution
The Tax Reform Act of 1986 and Statutory Partitioning

Congress originally enacted the federal research tax credit in 1981 to stimulate domestic technological investment and long-term economic advancement. In the years immediately following enactment, legislative oversight revealed that the initial statutory definition of qualified research was overly permissive, enabling taxpayers to claim tax credits for routine product development, aesthetic redesigns, and conventional software integration. To confine the fiscal subsidy strictly to genuine, high-technology innovation, Congress fundamentally restructured the statutory definition of qualified research through the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (TRA 1986), instituting the Business Component Test under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2).

The statutory architecture of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2) operates through three interconnected mechanisms that enforce component-level segmentation across all research claims. First, under the separate application mandate of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A), the qualification tests for qualified research must be applied separately to each discrete business component of the taxpayer. Second, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(B), Congress enumerated the six exclusive categories of a business component: any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business. Third, under the special production rule of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C), Congress mandated that any plant process, machinery, or technique for the commercial production of a business component must be treated as a separate and distinct business component, structurally partitioned from the end-product being manufactured.

By forcing taxpayers to segregate commercial production processes from product development under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C) and to isolate the exact component undergoing experimentation under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A), the statute enables the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and state taxing authorities to surgically exclude costs tied to routine integration, aesthetic styling, and sub-component construction that relies on established engineering parameters. Without this statutory partitioning, a manufacturer developing a novel chemical compound or beverage formula could improperly sweep routine factory automation or commercial production labor into the product's research pool, or vice versa. The legislative history recorded in House Conference Report No. 99-841 reinforces this statutory boundary, specifying that a "process of experimentation" requires the evaluation of more than one alternative designed to achieve a result where the capability or method of achieving that result is uncertain at the outset. Conference Report No. 99-841 confirms that evolutionary improvements and standard engineering modifications fall outside the scope of the statute; qualified research activities must fundamentally rely on the principles of the hard sciences to eliminate technical ambiguity.
Evolution of the Uncertainty Standard: From Treasury Decision 8930 to Treasury Decision 9104

Administrative interpretation of what constitutes technological uncertainty for a discrete business component shifted substantially between 2001 and 2004, altering the evidentiary threshold required to qualify a component. Under Treasury Decision 8930 (T.D. 8930, published in the Federal Register on January 3, 2001), the Treasury Department and the IRS enforced the restrictive "Discovery Rule". That regulatory standard required taxpayers to demonstrate that their research was undertaken to obtain knowledge that "exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in a particular field of science or engineering". By tying credit eligibility to macro-industry novelty, T.D. 8930 imposed a heightened evidentiary barrier that excluded applied engineering efforts unless the taxpayer could prove it was making novel, industry-altering discoveries.

Following sustained industry criticism and legal challenges demonstrating that the Discovery Rule conflicted with congressional intent, the Treasury Department promulgated final regulations under Treasury Decision 9104 (T.D. 9104, filed in December 2003, published in the Federal Register on January 2, 2004, and reported in Internal Revenue Bulletin 2004-6, effective for taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003). T.D. 9104 explicitly revoked the Discovery Rule and instituted a taxpayer-centric uncertainty threshold codified at 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(3). Under T.D. 9104, a taxpayer is not required to seek information that exceeds the current state of macro-industry knowledge; rather, uncertainty exists if the information available to the specific taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of the business component. Even when a taxpayer knows that achieving a technical objective is possible in principle, technological uncertainty legally exists under T.D. 9104 if the taxpayer is uncertain of the precise method or appropriate design needed to reach that goal.

This regulatory pivot produced a lasting shift in tax enforcement dynamics. Because taxing authorities could no longer summarily disqualify business components on the ground that the underlying scientific principles were already known within the broader engineering profession, administrative and judicial scrutiny migrated from macro-industry novelty to component-level substantiation of systematic experimentation and compliance with the 80% activity threshold under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4. T.D. 9104 remains the definitive, binding regulatory standard for evaluating whether a business component satisfies the uncertainty requirements of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d) across both federal and state R&D tax credit regimes.

Imposed an industry-wide novelty standard, disqualifying business components that adapted known scientific principles to taxpayer-specific engineering problems.

Shifted audit focus from macro-industry novelty to component-level substantiation of technical uncertainty and systematic experimentation under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4.

body.text: Integration Within the Four-Part Test of Qualified Research

The Business Component Test does not operate in isolation; it anchors the broader Four-Part Test codified in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1). For expenditures associated with any business component to yield QREs, all four statutory criteria must be satisfied sequentially, concurrently, and comprehensively for that specific discrete component. Precise statutory analysis requires reading the business component mandate of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(2) in conjunction with the qualified purpose definition in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3), and reading the process of experimentation mandate of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) alongside the regulatory definition of "substantially all" codified in 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6).

cells: Expenditures must be eligible for treatment as research or experimental expenditures under 26 U.S.C. § 174. The taxpayer must intend to discover information that would eliminate technical uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design for developing or improving the business component.
The process of discovering information for the business component must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

The taxpayer must intend to apply the discovered information to develop a new or improved business component. Under § 41(d)(3)(A)–(B), the purpose must relate to new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality, and cannot relate to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors.

"Substantially all" (defined by regulation as 80% or more) of the research activities measured on a cost or another consistently applied reasonable basis for the discrete business component must constitute elements of a process of experimentation involving hypotheses, evaluation of alternatives, and modeling or systematic trial and error.

body.text: Because 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A) requires the separate application of these four tests to each discrete business component, failure to substantiate any single prong—such as failing to document technological uncertainty for a specific software module under § 41(d)(1)(A) or failing to prove a systematic process of experimentation for an individual mechanical valve under § 41(d)(1)(C)—causes the complete disallowance of QREs associated with that component. Furthermore, the structural interdependence of these four prongs means that how a taxpayer defines the boundaries of the business component at the outset directly controls the denominator of the 80% Process of Experimentation calculation under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6).
Mechanics of the Shrinking-Back Rule (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2))
Structural Hierarchy and the 80% "Substantially All" Threshold

When a taxpayer develops a complex integrated system—such as a naval vessel, a manufacturing facility, an aircraft fuselage, or a multi-tiered enterprise software suite—the macro-level product frequently fails the Four-Part Test. Complex commercial projects typically require substantial routine construction, installation of off-the-shelf components, standard coding, or aesthetic design that dilutes the proportion of experimental activities relative to total project activities. Whenever these non-experimental activities exceed 20% of the total research activities on the overall component, the macro-level project fails the 80% "substantially all" Process of Experimentation threshold under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6).

To prevent the complete and inequitable disallowance of valid experimental research embedded within a larger commercial deliverable, the Department of the Treasury promulgated the "shrinking-back rule" under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2). Under this regulation, if the requirements of the Four-Part Test under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d) are not satisfied at the level of the discrete overall business component, the qualification tests are applied iteratively to the next most significant subset of elements of the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention. This shrinking-back cascade continues strictly down the structural hierarchy of the product—from the macro-system, to the sub-system, to the sub-assembly, and finally to the discrete part—until either a subset of elements satisfies all four statutory tests or the most basic element of the product is reached and fails.
Remedial Nature vs. Evidentiary Burden of Proof

A foundational principle of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2) is that the shrinking-back rule operates strictly as a remedial provision. It applies only if the overall product or macro-level component fails the Four-Part Test under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), and taxing authorities cannot weaponize the shrinking-back rule punitively to exclude valid research activities when an overall macro-component legitimately satisfies the 80% "substantially all" threshold. When a macro-component passes the 80% threshold, the remaining up to 20% of non-experimental research activities—along with incidental supply costs used in the development of the whole prototype—remain eligible within the qualified research framework. Conversely, if the macro-level component fails the 80% threshold, the evidentiary burden of proof rests entirely upon the taxpayer to substantiate the shrink-back.

This evidentiary asymmetry creates a decisive compliance risk in tax administration. To utilize the shrinking-back rule in an audit or judicial proceeding, the taxpayer must possess granular, contemporaneous project accounting that maps employee time, material costs, and experimental hypotheses strictly at the sub-component level. Taxpayers that adopt an "all or nothing" approach—treating a complex project as a single indivisible business component without maintaining sub-component time-tracking records—consistently lose in federal and state courts because the judiciary has no empirical basis upon which to compute the shrink-back. In such instances, the failure of the macro-level business component results in the total disallowance of the research credit claim.
Statutory Exclusions Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)

Even where a discrete business component theoretically satisfies the four-part qualification test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4) establishes categorical exclusions that disqualify associated expenditures from the research tax credit. First, under the adaptation exclusion of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(B), any research activity related to the adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need is strictly disqualified. When a company takes an existing software product or mechanical system and merely customizes the interface or integrates it into a client's specific server or operational environment using known coding or engineering parameters, the activity is statutorily excluded from qualified research.

Second, under the duplication and reverse engineering exclusion of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(C), any research related to the reproduction of an existing business component, in whole or in part, from a physical examination of the component itself or from plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information is statutorily excluded. Third, under the funded research exclusion of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), any research funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity does not qualify for the credit. To avoid disqualification under the funded research exclusion, a contractor or architectural and engineering (A&E) firm must prove through the governing contractual provisions that payment is contingent on the technical success of the research—meaning the taxpayer bears the economic risk of failure—and that the taxpayer retains substantial rights to the intellectual property developed.
Federal Judicial Precedent Governing the Business Component Test

Federal appellate and trial courts have rigorously enforced the component-level substantiation mandate of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2) and the mathematical constraints of the 80% Process of Experimentation test. Across federal circuits and the U.S. Tax Court, judicial review focuses on whether the taxpayer's contemporaneous records allow the tribunal to verify the 80% experimentation fraction at either the macro-project level or a properly isolated shrink-back tier.
Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner (7th Cir. 2023)

In Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit established binding appellate precedent governing the interaction between the 80% Process of Experimentation fraction and the shrinking-back rule. The taxpayer, a shipbuilding subsidiary, claimed research tax credits for the design and construction of large marine vessels, specifically a tanker barge and a dry dock. Throughout the examination and litigation, the taxpayer treated each entire vessel as a single, indivisible business component. The IRS disallowed the claims in full on the ground that the company failed to prove that "substantially all" (at least 80%) of the activities involved in the research constituted elements of a process of experimentation.

At the trial level, the U.S. Tax Court ruled against the taxpayer by adopting a highly restrictive formulation of the 80% fraction. The Tax Court unilaterally excluded the wages of production employees who physically built the pilot models, as well as the wages of direct supervisors, from the numerator of the experimentation test while pushing those massive labor pools entirely into the denominator. Because production and supervisory labor represented a substantial share of the shipbuilding effort, placing those hours solely in the denominator made it mathematically impossible for the shipbuilding projects to satisfy the 80% experimentation threshold at the macro level. When the taxpayer sought to invoke the shrinking-back rule to salvage QREs tied to specific novel sub-systems, the Tax Court refused, noting that the taxpayer had pursued an "all or nothing" legal strategy and completely failed to provide the component-level time tracking necessary for the court to calculate a shrink-back.

On appeal, the Seventh Circuit delivered a nuanced ruling that corrected the Tax Court's legal formulation of the 80% fraction while affirming the complete denial of the taxpayer's claim. Reversing the Tax Court's rigid mathematical exclusion of support and supervisory labor from the numerator, the Seventh Circuit held that the wages of personnel engaged in the "direct support" and "direct supervision" of research can legally be included in both the numerator and the denominator of the 80% test, provided those individuals are actively engaged in supporting or supervising genuine experimentation tasks:
Experimentation Fraction = (Direct Experimentation Activities + Qualifying Direct Supervision & Direct Support Activities) ÷ Total Research Activities Applied to the Business Component ≥ 80%

Despite lowering the legal barrier for what categories of labor may enter the numerator of the process of experimentation fraction, the Seventh Circuit affirmed the total denial of Little Sandy Coal's credits due to a catastrophic failure of documentation. Rather than maintaining a principled, contemporaneous breakdown of employee time by experimental activity at the sub-component level, the company relied on arbitrary departmental allocations, shortcut estimates, and opaque post-hoc testimony. The Seventh Circuit expressly warned that treating an entire marine vessel or building as an indivisible business component inherently blocks the application of the shrinking-back rule under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2), stripping the taxpayer of any ability to salvage qualifying sub-component activities.
Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States (N.D. Tex. 2010; 5th Cir. 2014)

The operational boundary between macro-level prototype qualification and failed shrink-back claims was similarly demonstrated in Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States, decided by the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas in 2010 and subsequently affirmed by the Fifth Circuit in 2014, 757 F.3d 400 (5th Cir. 2014). The substantive holding reflects the district court's project-by-project findings as affirmed on appellate review.

Trinity Industries sought research tax credits for the design and construction of six "first-in-class" prototype marine vessels. For two of the vessels, the district court allowed macro-level qualification, finding that the prototypes were so heavily experimental that the entire vessels qualified as creditable business components—including incidental supply costs such as paint and insurance—because non-qualified costs constituted less than 20% of the total project activities. This outcome illustrates the financial incentive that draws taxpayers toward macro-component claims: when non-experimental activities remain under the 20% ceiling, the entire macro-component's cost pool is swept into eligibility.

For the remaining four vessel projects, however, where evidence of novelty was less pervasive and non-experimental activities exceeded 20%, the taxpayer lost entirely. Trinity Industries had utilized the same "all or nothing" accounting structure later rejected in Little Sandy Coal. Because Trinity failed to produce sub-component time-tracking and engineering cost data, the district court was legally unable to apply the shrinking-back rule under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2) to isolate the experimental aspects of those four ship design projects, explicitly noting that it applied the 80% rule only to entire projects due to an absolute lack of evidence permitting a shrink-back calculation.
Betz v. Commissioner (T.C. 2023) and Phoenix Design Group v. Commissioner (T.C. 2024)

Recent U.S. Tax Court decisions have further reinforced the evidentiary supremacy of contemporaneous scientific documentation over broad engineering assertions. In Betz v. Commissioner (decided by the Tax Court in July 2023), the taxpayer submitted vague, opaque testimony regarding the development of hydrogen/oxidizer units and attempted to claim the units as experimental pilot models. The Tax Court rejected the claim in full, noting the complete failure to document technological uncertainty or a systematic process of experimentation. Ruling that the units were standard commercial end-products rather than prototypes utilized to test design alternatives, the court emphasized that the absence of documented hypotheses and test logs was fatal to the claim.

Similarly, in Phoenix Design Group v. Commissioner (decided by the Tax Court in December 2024), the court ruled that standard engineering design does not inherently equate to a process of experimentation under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C). The taxpayer treated all projects generically using broad sampling without conducting any sub-component analysis. The Tax Court disallowed the credits in their entirety, holding that broad statistical or project sampling without project-level and component-level scientific narratives fails the statutory standard of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d).
United States v. Davenport (N.D. Tex. 2013)

The strict enforcement of the adaptation exclusion within the Business Component Test was heavily litigated in United States v. Davenport, No. 3:2009cv02455 (N.D. Tex. 2013), an action brought by the federal government to recover erroneously issued tax refunds related to the implementation of a J.D. Edwards OneWorld software application suite. The taxpayers argued that their customization and implementation of the software involved a complex process of custom design and testing that satisfied the Four-Part Test.

The district court ruled in favor of the government, holding that the project was merely the adaptation of existing commercially available enterprise resource planning (ERP) software to a specific customer's needs, strictly triggering the adaptation exclusion under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(B). Furthermore, when the taxpayers argued that the court should apply the shrinking-back rule under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2) to isolate custom-coded sub-modules, the court rejected the argument, noting that the taxpayers had completely failed to identify the "next discrete possible business component" or provide evidence demonstrating how that specific sub-component independently constituted qualified research.

body.text: State-Level Conformity and Enforcement Frameworks

While 26 U.S.C. § 41 defines the federal parameters of the research credit, individual states frequently conform to this statutory definition while imposing their own geographic nexus, administrative, and evidentiary mandates. Executive interpretations and judicial rulings in Indiana, California, and Idaho illustrate how state taxing authorities enforce the Business Component Test and the shrinking-back rule in parallel with federal appellate courts.

body.text: The Indiana Framework: IDOR Letters of Findings and Tell City Boatworks

The Indiana Research Expense Credit (REC) is established under Indiana Code (IC) 6-3.1-4 et seq., which incorporates the federal definition of adjusted gross income subject to state modifications and explicitly adopts the federal definition of "qualified research" under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d). Consequently, a taxpayer claiming the Indiana REC must satisfy the exact same Four-Part Test, identify discrete business components, and adhere to the shrinking-back rule, with the primary state modification that QREs must be incurred for research conducted physically within the geographic boundaries of Indiana. Because Indiana is situated within the federal Seventh Circuit, the appellate standards articulated in Little Sandy Coal directly reinforce the audit practices of the Indiana Department of Revenue (IDOR).

The IDOR enforces an aggressive audit methodology that relies heavily on the IRS Audit Techniques Guide to demand project-level and component-level accounting, consistently disallowing credits in their entirety when taxpayers utilize high-level percentage estimates or retrospective labor allocations. In an administrative Letter of Findings concerning an Indiana brewery, the IDOR rejected an R&D study prepared by a consultant because the time-tracking records did not represent actual contemporaneous time spent by employees on specific sub-components. The IDOR observed that while creating new beer recipes might involve uncertainty under the standard of T.D. 9104, standard brewing production processes utilizing those ingredients do not qualify, and the failure to segregate experimental labor from commercial production labor via the Business Component Test (specifically 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C)) was fatal to the claim. Similarly, in an audit of a general construction contractor, the IDOR ruled that technical activities involving little uncertainty—where personnel simply apply their standard professional credentials to a known environment—are non-qualifying activities.

The definitive state-level judicial interpretation in Indiana is the Indiana Tax Court's decision in Tell City Boatworks, Inc. v. Indiana Department of State Revenue, 162 N.E.3d 603 (Ind. Tax Ct. 2020). Tell City Boatworks, a custom boat builder, claimed Indiana RECs for six vessel construction projects. Following an IDOR audit denial and a five-day trial, the Indiana Tax Court affirmed the disallowance in full. Analyzing each vessel as a discrete business component, the court conceded that some projects met the Section 174 intent test and the Technological in Nature test, but held that the taxpayer fundamentally failed the Process of Experimentation test under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C). Tell City argued that its iterative design process was experimental, but the court found that the company did not design the vessels from scratch and instead made "standard modifications to existing designs and/or incorporated well-known capabilities". Because Tell City failed the test at the macro level of the entire vessel and lacked the granular, contemporaneous documentation required to prove scientific trial and error at the subsystem level, the Indiana Tax Court was legally barred from applying the shrinking-back rule, leaving the taxpayer with zero allowable credits.
The California Framework: Appeal of Walden and Appeal of Abramson

The State of California establishes its research credit for corporate taxpayers under California Revenue and Taxation Code (RTC) § 23609 and for personal income taxpayers under RTC § 17052.12. California strictly conforms to the federal rules of 26 U.S.C. § 41, subject to the geographic constraint that qualified research must be conducted strictly within California. The California Franchise Tax Board (FTB) audits these claims aggressively, generating a substantial body of administrative precedent before the California Office of Tax Appeals (OTA).

In the Appeal of Walden, et al. (2018-OTA-209), the taxpayers claimed California research credits for the engineering of customized modular buildings. The FTB conceded that the "technological in nature" test was satisfied under the relaxed standards of T.D. 9104—acknowledging that the Discovery Rule was no longer in force—but challenged the claim under the Business Component and Process of Experimentation tests. Asserting that the structural engineering involved was routine work common within the modular building industry, the FTB argued that integrating known project parameters into a functional building did not constitute a process of experimentation. The OTA focused its analysis on the taxpayer's burden to define the exact business component and prove that specific experiments were conducted on that component to resolve technical uncertainty.

In the Appeal of Abramson, et al. (2024-OTA-636 Nonprecedential), the taxpayers attempted to rely on witness testimony and generic timesheets to substantiate their claimed work hours for the California research credit. Following the FTB's denial, the OTA heavily cited the federal Seventh Circuit decision in Little Sandy Coal, affirming that broad assertions and generic timesheets are insufficient to satisfy the 80% "substantially all" rule or the strict recordkeeping requirements of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d). When the taxpayers pleaded for the OTA to apply the shrinking-back rule to salvage sub-component activities, the OTA refused, holding that because the taxpayers failed to provide granular records mapping specific activities to specific sub-components, it was legally impossible for the tribunal to apply the shrink-back rule. This cross-citation demonstrates how federal appellate precedent from the Seventh Circuit rapidly propagates into state administrative tribunals across the country.
The Idaho Framework: Activity-Based Measurement and the Adaptation Exclusion

The Idaho State Tax Commission enforces strict conformity to the federal Four-Part Test under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d) for Idaho Affected Business Entity (ABE) returns. In Idaho State Tax Commission Docket No. 1-707-713-536, an Idaho taxpayer protested the disallowance of research credits claimed for "Website Development" and "3D Modeling" projects. The Commission upheld the disallowance because the projects failed to satisfy both the Business Component Test and the Process of Experimentation Test.

In its ruling, the Idaho State Tax Commission emphasized that the 80% "substantially all" test must be applied to research activities rather than physical elements, noting that the extent of experimentation does not vary merely in proportion to the physical size of an element. Furthermore, the Commission strictly enforced the statutory exclusions of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4), ruling that standard website development and 3D modeling utilizing existing commercial software engines routinely fall under the "adaptation of an existing business component" exclusion of § 41(d)(4)(B), rendering the activities disqualified regardless of the level of effort expended by the taxpayer.
Contemporaneous Documentation Standards and IRS Audit Techniques Guide

The overarching mandate across all federal and state jurisdictions is the absolute necessity of contemporaneous documentation. The IRS Audit Techniques Guide—including specialized industry directives such as the Aerospace Industry Audit Techniques Guide (January 2005), which serves as the operational manual for federal agents and state auditors alike—explicitly dictates how examiners evaluate research tax credit claims. The Guide emphasizes that taxpayers must tie every single dollar of claimed QRE directly to a specifically identified business component. To survive audit scrutiny and prevent total disallowance of credits, businesses must proactively generate an auditable digital paper trail at the time the research is conducted rather than reconstructing estimates retroactively years later during an audit defense.

A compliant substantiation architecture must integrate four core categories of contemporaneous records. First, taxpayers must maintain project charters and statements of work detailing the specific technical uncertainties regarding capability, method, or design faced at the outset of the project. Second, engineering teams must preserve scientific and engineering logs—including test protocols, modeling records, and empirical data analysis—showing the formulation of hypotheses and systematic trial-and-error experimentation. Third, payroll systems and timesheets must capture granular time-tracking data that maps hours not merely to a macro-project, but to specific experimental tasks tied to discrete sub-components, such as separating hours spent on routine structural welding from hours spent on stress-testing a novel alloy joint. Fourth, third-party contractors and A&E firms operating under fixed-price contracts must maintain thorough contractual analyses demonstrating provisions that explicitly link payment to the technical success of the research (proving the taxpayer bears the economic risk of failure) alongside clauses guaranteeing that the taxpayer retains substantial intellectual property rights under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H).
Hypothetical Worked Examples: Component Segmentation and Shrink-Back Computation

To clarify the exact operational and mathematical mechanics of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2), the 80% "substantially all" threshold of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6), and the iterative shrinking-back rule of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2), the following two hypothetical worked examples model aerospace manufacturing and enterprise software scenarios using step-by-step activity calculations.
Hypothetical Worked Example 1: Aerospace Manufacturing (Commercial Drone Hydraulic Actuator)

Consider a hypothetical aerospace manufacturer contracted to design a next-generation commercial drone fuselage. The overall macro-project (the entire drone) utilizes a conventional aerodynamic shell, standard commercial lithium-ion batteries, and off-the-shelf navigational software. To achieve extreme high-altitude operation, however, the company's engineers must design a radically new hydraulic actuator for the landing gear using an unproven polymer composite.

Assume the manufacturer incurs 10,000 total engineering and fabrication labor hours ($1,000,000 in total wage and supply expenditures) across the entire macro-drone project. Within that total, routine integration of the aerodynamic shell, commercial lithium-ion batteries, and off-the-shelf navigation software consumes 7,500 hours ($750,000) with 0% experimental activity; routine engineering of the standard mechanical struts within the landing gear sub-system consumes 1,500 hours ($150,000) with 0% experimental activity; and thermal design, iterative hypothesis evaluation, and destructive testing of the unproven polymer composite hydraulic actuator consume 1,000 hours ($100,000), representing 100% experimental activity.
When the qualification tests are applied first at the Macro System Level (the entire commercial drone) under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A), the macro experimentation fraction is computed as follows:
Macro Experimentation Fraction = 1,000 experimental hours ÷ 10,000 total project hours = 10.0%

Because 10.0% is well below the 80% "substantially all" threshold of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6)—with routine integration and non-experimental activities accounting for 90.0% of total project hours, far exceeding the 20% maximum tolerance—the overall drone fails the Process of Experimentation test at the macro level. If the taxpayer logged all 10,000 hours under a single generic "Drone Project" accounting code, the audit inquiry terminates here and $0 in QREs are allowed.

Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2), however, if the taxpayer maintained sub-component accounting, the evaluation shrinks back from the macro drone to the next most significant subset of elements: the Landing Gear Sub-System (comprising the 1,500 hours on standard mechanical struts plus the 1,000 hours on the hydraulic actuator, totaling 2,500 hours and $250,000). Recomputing the experimentation fraction at the sub-system tier yields:
Sub-System Experimentation Fraction = 1,000 experimental hours ÷ (1,500 strut hours + 1,000 actuator hours) = 1,000 ÷ 2,500 = 40.0%

Because 40.0% < 80%, the Landing Gear Sub-System also fails the "substantially all" test due to the inclusion of the standard struts, triggering a second iterative shrink-back to the Hydraulic Actuator Sub-Assembly. At this granular sub-assembly level—where engineers logged all 1,000 hours ($100,000 in wages and destructive-testing material supplies) specifically to a dedicated "Polymer Actuator Thermal Testing" project code to resolve technical uncertainty regarding the polymer's performance under extreme cold—the experimentation fraction is:
Sub-Assembly Experimentation Fraction = 1,000 experimental hours ÷ 1,000 total actuator hours = 100.0%

Because 100.0% ≥ 80% and the actuator independently satisfies the Section 174 uncertainty, Technological in Nature, and Permitted Purpose criteria, the Hydraulic Actuator Sub-Assembly qualifies as a discrete business component under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2), cleanly isolating and preserving $100,000 in QREs against federal and state audit scrutiny.
Hypothetical Worked Example 2: Enterprise Software Architecture (Backend Encryption Algorithm)

Consider a hypothetical cybersecurity firm developing a commercial enterprise software suite. The macro-level software release utilizes standard user-interface (UI) dashboards, routine database query languages, and standard data-storage protocols, while deep within the backend architecture the firm's engineers develop a novel, proprietary encryption algorithm intended to isolate and neutralize network intrusions without causing false-positive system downtime.

Assume the software engineering team logs 5,000 total coding and testing hours ($600,000 in wage expenditures) across the software suite. Standard UI dashboard coding consumes 2,200 hours ($264,000) with 0% experimental activity, and routine database query and storage protocol integration consumes 1,800 hours ($216,000) with 0% experimental activity. Within the 1,000 total hours ($120,000 in wages) dedicated to the backend encryption algorithm module, engineers spend 850 hours conducting iterative algorithm hypothesis modeling and trial-and-error testing, 100 hours in direct supervision and direct support of that encryption experimentation (qualifying for both the numerator and denominator under the Seventh Circuit's holding in Little Sandy Coal), and 50 hours on routine post-validation code formatting, yielding 950 qualifying experimental hours.

If the cybersecurity firm claims the entire software suite as a single macro-level business component, the vast volume of routine UI and database coding dilutes the experimentation fraction well below 80%:
Macro Experimentation Fraction = 950 qualifying experimental hours ÷ 5,000 total suite hours = 19.0%

Because 19.0% < 80%, the macro-level software suite fails the Process of Experimentation test. If the firm tracked all engineering hours solely to a generic "Version 2.0 Development" bucket, the IRS will deny the shrink-back for lack of substantiation and all credits will be lost. Conversely, because the software engineers utilized agile tracking software (such as Jira) to tag their coding and testing hours contemporaneously to dedicated "Encryption Algorithm Iteration" tickets, the firm can invoke 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2) during an examination to shrink the business component back past the UI and database modules directly to the Backend Encryption Algorithm Module (1,000 total module hours; $120,000 module wages):
Module Experimentation Fraction = (850 direct experimental hours + 100 direct support/supervision hours) ÷ 1,000 total module hours = 950 ÷ 1,000 = 95.0%

Because 95.0% ≥ 80%, the Backend Encryption Algorithm Module satisfies the "substantially all" threshold under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6), allowing the firm to isolate and substantiate the qualifying experimental wages tied to the encryption module.

body.text: Analytical Synthesis and Compliance Conclusions

The Business Component Test under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2) and its implementing shrinking-back regulation under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2) serve as the uncompromising structural foundation of the federal and state R&D tax credit framework, prohibiting the blending of routine commercial development with genuine technological innovation. Defining a business component at the macro-project level maximizes the potential pool of QREs—capturing incidental supplies and integration labor when non-experimental activities remain below 20%, as demonstrated by the two qualifying prototype vessels in Trinity Industries—but exposes the taxpayer to catastrophic cliff-edge disallowance whenever routine activities exceed 20%.

As confirmed across federal and state tribunals in Little Sandy Coal, Trinity Industries, Davenport, Betz, Phoenix Design Group, Tell City Boatworks, Appeal of Walden, Appeal of Abramson, and Idaho Docket No. 1-707-713-536, the shrinking-back rule cannot be invoked as a post-hoc legal argument during an audit or litigation unless the taxpayer's underlying project accounting already segments labor and supply costs by sub-system and sub-assembly. To secure and defend research tax credits across federal and state jurisdictions, modern enterprises must embed tax-compliance tracking directly into their engineering and scientific workflows, proactively identifying the discrete locus of technical uncertainty at the outset of a project, segmenting business components accordingly, and generating contemporaneous documentation of the iterative trial-and-error process.
